## Geometric Motivation for the Monge Cone

### Setup

Consider the general first-order PDE

$$F(x, y, u, p, q) = 0, \qquad p = u_x,\; q = u_y.$$

A $C^1$ solution $u = u(x,y)$ defines an **integral surface** $S \subset \mathbb{R}^3$ via $z = u(x,y)$. At a point $P_0 = (x_0, y_0, z_0)$ on $S$, the tangent plane is

$$\Pi:\quad z - z_0 = p\,(x - x_0) + q\,(y - y_0), \tag{1}$$

with normal vector $(p, q, -1)$. The pair $(p,q)$ is not free: it must satisfy the PDE constraint

$$F(x_0, y_0, z_0, p, q) = 0. \tag{2}$$

### The family of admissible tangent planes

At the fixed point $P_0$, equations (1)–(2) define a **one-parameter family of planes** through $P_0$: the constraint (2) removes one degree of freedom from the two parameters $(p,q)$, leaving a single free parameter (say $p$, with $q$ determined implicitly by (2) when $F_q \neq 0$).

### The Monge cone as the envelope

The **envelope** of this one-parameter family of planes is, by construction, a **cone with vertex at $P_0$**. This is the *Monge cone* at $P_0$.

To see it is a cone (i.e., every element is a ray from $P_0$): each plane in the family passes through $P_0$, so the envelope — being the locus where consecutive planes of the family meet — also passes through $P_0$, and by homogeneity of the construction (scaling $(x-x_0, y-y_0, z-z_0)$ leaves (1) invariant), the envelope is invariant under scaling about $P_0$. Hence it is a cone.

Concretely, parameterize the family by $p$ (with $q = q(p)$ from (2)). The envelope is obtained by eliminating $p$ between

$$z - z_0 = p\,(x-x_0) + q(p)\,(y-y_0) \tag{1'}$$

and its $p$-derivative

$$0 = (x - x_0) + q'(p)\,(y - y_0). \tag{3}$$

Since $F_p + q'(p)\,F_q = 0$ (differentiating (2) in $p$), equation (3) gives

$$\frac{x - x_0}{F_q} = \frac{y - y_0}{-F_p},$$

and substituting back yields the **characteristic (Monge) strip equations**

$$\frac{dx}{F_p} = \frac{dy}{F_q} = \frac{dz}{p\,F_p + q\,F_q}. \tag{4}$$

The directions $(F_p, F_q, pF_p + qF_q)$, as $(p,q)$ ranges over the curve (2), sweep out the **generators of the Monge cone**.

### How it visualizes solution surfaces

The Monge cone at $P_0$ encodes **all directions in which an integral surface may pass through $P_0$**. A solution surface $S$ through $P_0$ must satisfy:

1. Its tangent plane at $P_0$ is one of the admissible planes (1)–(2) — i.e., it is a plane of the family generating the cone.
2. Equivalently, $S$ is **tangent to the Monge cone** at $P_0$: the tangent plane of $S$ contains a generator of the cone (the generator along which the envelope touches that particular plane).

Thus, along a solution surface, at every point the surface is tangent to the local Monge cone. The surface is "knit together" from generators of the cones along it. The generators (4) are the **characteristic directions**, and integrating them yields the characteristic strips whose envelopes form the integral surface. This is the geometric content of the Cauchy–Kowalewski / Monge method: solve the characteristic ODE system

$$\dot x = F_p,\quad \dot y = F_q,\quad \dot z = pF_p + qF_q,\quad \dot p = -F_x - pF_u,\quad \dot q = -F_y - qF_u,$$

and envelope the resulting family of characteristic strips.

### The quasi-linear case

A **quasi-linear** first-order PDE has the form

$$F(x,y,u,p,q) = a(x,y,u)\,p + b(x,y,u)\,q - c(x,y,u) = 0. \tag{5}$$

Here $F$ is *linear* in $(p,q)$. The constraint (2) becomes a single **linear** equation $a\,p + b\,q = c$ in the $(p,q)$-plane — a line. The corresponding family of tangent planes (1) now has a special property: **every plane in the family contains a common direction**.

Indeed, a direction $(dx, dy, dz)$ lies in the tangent plane (1) iff $dz = p\,dx + q\,dy$. Choosing the direction $(a, b, c)$:

$$p\,a + q\,b = c \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad a\,p + b\,q = c,$$

which is exactly the PDE (5). Therefore **every admissible tangent plane contains the direction $(a, b, c)$** (evaluated at $P_0$).

Consequently the one-parameter family of planes does not sweep out a genuine cone — all its planes share the common line through $P_0$ in direction $(a,b,c)$, and the envelope **degenerates to a single line (a single generator)**:

$$\boxed{\text{Monge cone} \;\longrightarrow\; \text{single characteristic direction } (a, b, c).}$$

This is why quasi-linear first-order PDEs are markedly simpler:

- The Monge cone collapses to a **unique characteristic direction** $(a, b, c)$ at each point, rather than a one-parameter family of directions.
- There is no need to select among generators: the integral surface through $P_0$ must simply be tangent to the *single* direction $(a,b,c)$ at $P_0$.
- The characteristic system reduces to the ODE

$$\frac{dx}{a} = \frac{dy}{b} = \frac{dz}{c}, \tag{6}$$

which is a system for *curves* (the **characteristic curves**) in $\mathbb{R}^3$, decoupled from the $(p,q)$ equations. An integral surface is then the union of a one-parameter family of characteristic curves (6) issuing from an initial curve — the classical method of characteristics for quasi-linear equations.

### Summary

| | General nonlinear $F(x,y,u,p,q)=0$ | Quasi-linear $a\,p + b\,q = c$ |
|---|---|---|
| Constraint on $(p,q)$ | Curve $F=0$ in $(p,q)$-plane | Line $ap+bq=c$ in $(p,q)$-plane |
| Admissible tangent planes at $P_0$ | One-parameter family | One-parameter family, **all sharing a common direction** |
| Monge cone at $P_0$ | Genuine cone (one-parameter family of generators) | **Degenerates to a single line** in direction $(a,b,c)$ |
| Characteristic equations | Full 5D system (incl. $\dot p, \dot q$) | Reduced 3D system $dx/a = dy/b = dz/c$ |
| Construction of solution | Envelope of characteristic strips | Union of characteristic curves from initial data |

The Monge cone thus provides the geometric bridge between the algebraic constraint $F=0$ on the derivatives and the differential structure of integral surfaces: it packages, at each point, the totality of admissible tangent directions into a single geometric object, and the solution surface is recovered as a surface tangent to this cone at every point. In the quasi-linear case the cone's collapse to a line is precisely what makes the method of characteristics a straightforward ODE integration.
